<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and the clash genuinely narrowed. CON landed real damage: exposing that PRO's fixes are mostly "better" moderation rather than "more aggressive," extracting a "yes" on turning up an automated filter with appeals as the cure, and catching the tension between PRO's early "gate voice behind match history" and later "no day-one friction." But PRO built the cleaner decision rule and held it across every speech: harassment is a selection mechanism; CON's model leaves the proven slur-spammer in the game; a false strike is correctable while a driven-out player is not. CON's answer to "what happens to him" (reputation-weighted matching, introduced late) is itself a behavior-based consequence system that concedes much of PRO's frame, and CON's opt-in architecture was fairly characterized as either the motion relabeled or abdication with good UI. CON also suffered two clipped turns. PRO made the debate easier to decide and answered its pressure questions with clear A1/A2 concessions that were survivable, whereas CON's hardest problem—the abuser staying—was never squarely neutralized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2/[B4.4]–[B4.5]: forcing CON to name a consequence for the undefended slur-spammer, then framing CON's architecture as "a system that never wrongly silences anyone because it never silences anyone." CON's "loses his audience" reply was the weakest link in an otherwise strong case; CON's best counter was exposing PRO's "yes" on the unstaffed automated filter [A4.4].</best_rebuttal>
